About: The Vertical Circle — Where the String Nearly Lets Go

Source

Concept
In a vertical circle the tension varies round the loop; it is greatest at the bottom (speed largest, gravity opposing centripetal) and least at the top.
The one thing to notice
Tbottom − Ttop = 6 m g, no matter the speed or radius.
Serves
Newton's second law along the radius; energy conservation between top and bottom; the string-only-pulls constraint.
Misconception targeted
“The string is under most tension where the ball moves fastest, so both are at the bottom, and at the top gravity pulls the ball off the circle.”

Vertical Circle — string thickness tracks tension

Guided Inquiry

Step 1 · Predict — where does the string strain most?

The ball is swung in a vertical circle just fast enough to get round. Where on the circle is the string closest to snapping?

Step 2 · Watch the string

Press ▶ Play. Watch the string's thickness — it strains (thick and taut) at the bottom and goes slack (thin, curving) near the top. Read the tension number rising and falling with each pass.

The tension bar on the right shows the live value; zero is marked.

Step 3 · The invariant

Change the bottom speed. Change the radius. Watch Tbottom and Ttop both change — but what about their difference?

Step 4 · Free exploration

Drop the bottom speed toward the critical value. The top tension slides toward zero and the string goes slack at the top of the loop — the ball leaves the circle. Below the critical speed, it never gets to the top at all.

Play freely with both controls. The one thing to remember: Tbottom − Ttop = 6 m g, always.

The Physics

The Vertical Circle — Where the String Nearly Lets Go · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

A ball on a string is swung round a vertical circle. You choose its speed at the lowest point and the radius of the circle, and a bar on the right reads the tension in the string.

What you'll learn

  • Which forces act on the ball as it goes round.
  • How the pull in the string depends on where the ball is.
  • How fast the ball must go to complete the loop.
The ball moves on a circle of radius r. The speed vbot is set where the ball is lowest.

What's on screen

  • Ball (amber) on a string from the pivot. The dashed circle is its path, and the label under it gives r.
  • T (teal) points toward the centre and mg (orange) points straight down, both labelled in newtons. They show while the string is taut. The sim fixes m = 1 kg.
  • String: its thickness and colour follow the tension, and a slack string is drawn thin and curved. The tension bar on the right reads the same number, with its zero marked.
  • θ and v at the bottom left: the angle from the lowest point, and the ball's speed.

Fixed: the ball's mass m = 1 kg and g = 9.81 m/s². Moving a slider restarts the swing from the lowest point.

03

The tension at the bottom of the circle

At the lowest point the string pulls up, toward the centre, and gravity pulls down, away from it. Their difference is the inward force the circle needs.

T − mg = m vbot²/r
So Tbot = m vbot²/r + mg

Two effects add up here: the ball is at its fastest, and gravity works against the string. Higher up the ball slows, and above the side of the circle part of gravity points inward and helps the string.

With m = 1 kg, vbot = 9.95 m/s and r = 2 m: Tbot = 9.95²/2 + 9.81 = 49.50 + 9.81 = 59.31 N.

See itKeep the opening values and watch the bar for one lap. Watch for: the tension bar peaking at 59.3 N each time the ball passes the lowest point, and the bar falling low at the top.
04

Energy fixes the speed and the tension at every angle

Only gravity does work on the ball, because the string pulls at right angles to the motion. So the ball's kinetic energy falls by mgr(1 − cosθ) when it has climbed to the angle θ, measured from the lowest point.

v(θ)² = vbot² − 2gr(1 − cosθ)
T(θ) = m v(θ)²/r + mg cosθ
Together: T(θ) = m vbot²/r − 2mg + 3mg cosθ

At vbot = 9.95 m/s and r = 2 m the tension is 59.31 N at the bottom, 29.88 N at the side (θ = 90°, speed 7.73 m/s) and 0.45 N at the top (θ = 180°, speed 4.53 m/s).

Each quarter turn upward takes off the same 3mg = 29.43 N. The bottom-left label in the sim shows θ and v as the ball moves.

05

The bottom and top tensions compared

At the top, θ = 180°, so Ttop = m vbot²/r − 5mg. Subtract it from the bottom value, and the speed term cancels.

Tbot − Ttop = 6mg
Energy gives 4mg of the gap and the weight term gives 2mg. Neither v nor r is left.

For m = 1 kg that is 6 × 9.81 = 58.86 N. At vbot = 14 m/s and r = 1 m: Tbot = 205.81 N, Ttop = 146.95 N and the gap is again 58.86 N. This holds only while the loop is completed with the string taut.

These numbers follow the sim's sliders.

See itSet vbot = 14 m/s and r = 1 m. Watch for: the first readout still reading 58.86 N, equal to the line below it, though both tensions are far larger than before.
06

The least speed for a full loop is √(5gr)

A string can pull but not push, so Ttop cannot be negative. Ttop ≥ 0 means vtop² ≥ gr, and with vtop² = vbot² − 4gr this gives vbot ≥ √(5gr).

At r = 2 m the least speed is 9.90 m/s, and the sim opens at 9.95 m/s, just above it. That is why the top tension is only 0.45 N at the start. The least speed grows as √r: 7.00 m/s at 1 m and 12.13 m/s at 3 m. At that least speed the ball still moves at √(gr) at the top, 4.43 m/s here, not zero.

Below that speed the string goes slack on the way up. At vbot = 9.0 m/s and r = 2 m this happens about 135° from the bottom, and the ball leaves the circle as a projectile.

See itSet vbot = 9.0 m/s with r = 2 m. Watch for: the label "string SLACK" at about 135°, the bar falling to 0, the ball leaving the circle, and the note quoting 9.90 m/s.
07

Where it matters

  • Swinging a bucket of water. The water stays in at the top only if the bucket is moving at √(gr) or faster there. Below that, the bottom of the bucket can no longer press on the water.
  • Roller-coaster loops. The track can only push, as the string can only pull. For a small car the same condition, vbot ≥ √(5gr), keeps it on the track at the top.
  • Pilots in a loop. At the bottom the seat pushes with more than the pilot's weight, and at the top with the least force of the whole loop.
08

Summary

In one line. The sim swings a ball on a string in a vertical circle and reads out the tension as you change the speed at the lowest point and the radius.

Key points

  • T(θ) = m v(θ)²/r + mg cosθ, with v(θ)² = vbot² − 2gr(1 − cosθ).
  • The tension is greatest at the bottom and least at the top.
  • Tbot − Ttop = 6mg for any completed loop.
  • The least bottom speed for a full loop is √(5gr).

Common mix-ups

  • "The string is most strained where the ball is slowest." At the top the ball is slowest, but gravity then helps the string. The bottom is worst.
  • "At the top the speed can fall to zero." It cannot fall below √(gr) and still keep the string taut.
  • "mv²/r is another force on the ball." It is the net inward force, made up of T and the weight.

Things to try on your own

  • Set r = 3 m and vbot = 12.2 m/s. Check that the gap is still 58.86 N.
  • At r = 1 m, find the speed where the loop first completes (7.00 m/s).
  • Raise vbot to 18 m/s and compare Tbot with Ttop.
